\section{Discussion}
\label{sec:discussion}

The central finding is that recursive generation alters \emph{where} the NLL distribution sits but not \emph{how} it is shaped.
Under fixed temperature $\tau$ and nucleus $p$, decoding configuration constrains the softmax output distribution's shape, while iterative conditioning shifts the input distribution's location; temperature may act as a shape control parameter that bounds entropy spread and explains both high-temperature degradation and shape-feature stability.
This interpretation is post-hoc; formal analysis remains open.
DDR is a parameter-dependent empirical decomposition, not a universal property of recursive generation: ablations (\S\ref{sec:results-differential}) show degradation at $t{=}0.9$ ($-9.3$ to $-26.0$\,pp) and variation across prompt types.

Several boundary conditions constrain practical applicability.
Instruction tuning alters the depth signal across all three tested families (Appendix~\ref{app:instruct}): entropy-mean $\rho$ reverses sign ($-0.6$ base $\rightarrow$ $+0.23$ to $+0.48$ instruct), the DDR partition degrades (silhouette: 0.632 $\rightarrow$ 0.338; cross-condition transfer near chance), and retraining partially recovers within-model binary F1 ($+$7--27\,pp) but remains below base-model levels, restricting the structured partition to base models.
Cross-temperature transfer degrades at $t{=}1.0$ (Appendix~\ref{app:cross-temp}); a downstream pilot (Appendix~\ref{app:downstream}) does not detect a depth-composition effect, though $n{=}3$ seeds is insufficient for conclusions.

DDR occupies a specific position in the landscape of recursive generation analysis.
The QLoRA end-to-end classifier (3-class F1\,=\,0.905, 6-generator LOGO; Appendix~\ref{app:qlora}) confirms richer representations capture depth signal beyond the 7-feature set; the handcrafted ensemble trades classification ceiling for the interpretability that enables DDR decomposition.
QLoRA on instruct data further confirms this gap: 3-class F1 recovers to 0.89--0.91 (vs.\ XGBoost retrain 0.58--0.73; Appendix~\ref{app:instruct}), indicating that instruction tuning reorganizes rather than eliminates the depth signal.
Three classes represent the practical ceiling (5-class F1 ${\approx}$0.50; Appendix~\ref{app:finer-depth}), with simulated editing suggesting graceful degradation (Appendix~\ref{app:human-edit}).
DDR is distinct from model collapse \cite{curse_of_recursion,strong_model_collapse}: unlike training-loop collapse, which irreversibly erodes distributional coverage through parameter updates, inference-chain drift under fixed parameters is fully reversible and leaves distributional shape near-stationary ($d < 0.10$; variance ratios 0.98--1.12).

To assess whether the DDR three-way partition generalizes beyond the default temperature ($\tau{=}0.7$), we computed per-feature Cohen's $d$ (generation~1 vs.\ generation~2+) at $\tau \in \{0.5, 0.7, 0.9\}$ for all four generators in the temperature ablation (12 conditions total; Table~\ref{tab:ddr-temp-stability}).

\centering

\label{tab:ddr-temp-stability}
\begin{tabular}{lccc l}
\toprule
\textbf{Feature} & $\boldsymbol{\tau{=}0.5}$ & $\boldsymbol{\tau{=}0.7}$ & $\boldsymbol{\tau{=}0.9}$ & \textbf{Group} \\
\midrule

\midrule

The partition anchors are robust: entropy mean remains drifting in all 12 conditions, TTR in 10/12, and hapax ratio in 9/12; entropy min and entropy max stay near-stationary in 10/12 and 9/12 conditions, respectively.
The two boundary features are more temperature-sensitive: entropy std is drifting at $\tau{=}0.5$ for all generators but falls to intermediate at $\tau{=}0.9$ for three of four, while tail decay fluctuates between near-stationary and intermediate across generators.
Effect sizes compress monotonically with temperature: for the fixed drifting set (entropy mean, TTR, hapax ratio), mean $|d|$ drops from 1.09 at $\tau{=}0.5$ to 0.90 at $\tau{=}0.7$ to 0.48 at $\tau{=}0.9$, shifting individual features across partition boundaries at high temperature without altering the qualitative hierarchy: lexical diversity features drift fastest, entropy extrema remain stable across all conditions tested.

\section{Results}
\label{sec:results}

\subsection{Depth Classification Performance}
\label{sec:results-classification}

Generation depth proves classifiable across diverse architectures: the 7-feature ensemble achieves 3-class LOGO F1\,=\,0.762 (95\% CI [0.758, 0.766]; $N$\,=\,37{,}058) across eight generators from five families (Table~\ref{tab:logo-results}).
Because gen-0 seeds are shared across generators (\S\ref{sec:generation}), gen-0 classification is near-perfect (per-class F1\,$\approx$\,0.94) and the 3-class metric is inflated by this overlap.
We therefore adopt leak-free binary F1 (gen-1 vs.\ gen-2+)\,=\,0.694, CI [0.688, 0.700], as the primary metric throughout; it excludes gen-0 entirely and is unaffected by seed sharing.
Per-generator binary F1 ranges from 0.633 (Mistral-7B) to 0.724 (Pythia-2.8B), with the primary difficulty being gen-1 vs.\ gen-2+ discrimination (Appendix~\ref{app:confusion}).

\paragraph{Cross-model generalization.}
Cross-model chains (randomly selected generator per step) yield binary F1\,=\,0.764 under 5-fold CV.\footnote{Cross-model chains use the original five-generator subset (Pythia, OLMo, Qwen); Llama and Mistral were added later for single-generator evaluation. Sample-level CV is used because each chain contains multiple generators, making generator-level held-out splits inapplicable. Sample-level splits may introduce within-chain correlation; chain-level (seed-level) validation remains open.}
The higher cross-model F1 (vs.\ 0.694 single-generator LOGO) may reflect generator heterogeneity amplifying depth-correlated distributional shifts; generator identity information in mixed chains could partially confound the depth signal.
A single-generator transfer analysis (Appendix~\ref{app:transfer}) provides evidence against this confound: classifiers trained on one generator transfer to all seven others with mean binary F1\,=\,0.810 (95\% CI [0.796, 0.822]), significantly above chance.
Leave-one-family-out (LOFO) evaluation yields binary F1\,=\,0.686, consistent with cross-family transfer.
A scale effect emerges: Pythia generators achieve the highest binary F1 (0.718--0.724), while larger models show degradation (Mistral-7B: 0.633), partly reflecting same-family affinity with the Pythia-410M reference model (cross-reference spread $\leq$0.013; \S\ref{sec:results-differential}).
Preliminary cross-domain evaluation suggests the signal persists with variation, though a domain$\times$temperature interaction exists (Appendix~\ref{app:domain}).
An end-to-end QLoRA classifier achieves 3-class F1\,=\,0.905 (6-generator LOGO; $+$11.6\,pp; Appendix~\ref{app:qlora}), which indicates that richer representations capture additional depth signal beyond the 7-feature set; on instruct data, QLoRA recovers to 0.89--0.91 (Appendix~\ref{app:instruct}).

\paragraph{Length confound control.}
Length-matched subsampling yields binary F1\,=\,0.724 (vs.\ 0.770 unmatched); a random-subsample control confirms the drop reflects deconfounding, not sample-size reduction (Appendix~\ref{app:length}).

\paragraph{Seed-sharing control.}
Seed-level demeaning (F1\,=\,0.701) and an independent-seed experiment with disjoint seed pools (F1\,=\,0.680; Appendix~\ref{app:seed-control}) both confirm the classifier captures generative degradation, not seed-specific content.

\subsection{Differential Depth Response}
\label{sec:results-differential}

Features exhibit a continuous gradient of depth sensitivity, with a data-driven binary partition as the strongest structure: $k{=}2$ clustering in standardized $(|\rho|, d)$ space yields silhouette\,=\,0.632 (Appendix~\ref{app:ddr-validation}), separating \emph{drifting} features (entropy mean, TTR, hapax ratio; $|\rho| > 0.60$, $d{=}0.76$--$1.17$) from \emph{non-drifting} ones.
We use the shorthand \emph{differential depth response} (DDR) for this partition and further resolve a 3/1/3 characterization using domain-informed criteria: entropy std occupies a sole \emph{intermediate} position (large level shift $d{=}0.55$, low monotonicity $|\rho|{=}0.16$); the remaining three \emph{near-stationary} features (entropy max, tail decay, entropy min) show negligible depth effects ($d < 0.10$; CV shift $<$3\% vs.\ $>$15\% for drifting).
This partition is robust under heteroscedasticity-corrected metrics (below).

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{fig1_differential_response.pdf}
\caption{Differential depth response: Spearman correlations between individual features and generation depth. Drifting features (hapax ratio, TTR, entropy mean) show $|\rho| > 0.60$; entropy std ($|\rho|{=}0.16$, $d{=}0.55$) is the sole intermediate feature; near-stationary features (entropy max, tail decay, entropy min) show $d < 0.10$ for gen-1 vs.\ gen-2+ (entropy min's elevated pooled $|\rho|$ reflects the gen-0/gen-1 boundary; \S\ref{sec:results-differential}).}
\label{fig:feature-drift}
\end{figure}

Pooled class-balanced Spearman correlations with depth confirm the split (Figure~\ref{fig:feature-drift}):
drifting features show substantial monotonic trends (hapax ratio $\rho = -0.64$, TTR $\rho = -0.63$, entropy mean $\rho = -0.60$),
while shape features remain near-stationary (tail decay $|\rho| = 0.04$; per-depth distributions in Appendix~\ref{app:feature-distributions}).
The six-fold magnitude gap between drifting ($|\rho| > 0.60$) and near-stationary features ($|\rho| < 0.10$) defines the DDR partition, with entropy std ($|\rho| = 0.16$, $d{=}0.55$) as the sole intermediate member.
The 3/1/3 partition is stable across $d$ thresholds in $[0.56, 0.75]$; data-driven clustering confirms the primary drifting/non-drifting split ($k{=}2$, silhouette\,=\,0.632; Appendix~\ref{app:ddr-validation}).

\paragraph{Distributional shift quantification.}
Two-sample KS tests confirm the split: drifting-feature statistics (0.516--0.537) are ${\sim}10\times$ larger than shape-feature statistics (0.043--0.052; all $p \approx 0$ after Bonferroni correction).
Cohen's $d$ \cite{cohen1988statistical} (pooled, class-balanced) converges with $\rho$: drifting features show large effects (entropy mean $d{=}1.17$, TTR $d{=}0.88$, hapax ratio $d{=}0.76$), while shape features are near zero (entropy max $d{=}0.08$, tail decay $d{=}0.08$).
Levene tests reject strict equal-variance ($p < 10^{-10}$); Glass's $\Delta$ (using gen-1 SD) amplifies drifting effects (entropy mean $\Delta{=}1.41$, hapax $\Delta{=}0.94$) while near-stationary features remain negligible ($\Delta \leq 0.10$), yielding a ${\geq}9.5\times$ gap. Cliff's $\delta$ corroborates the partition (Appendix~\ref{app:ddr-validation}).
Shape-feature CV shift ($<$3\% vs.\ $>$15\% for drifting features) supports ``near-stationary'' as a practical characterization.
Five features fall cleanly into the drifting or near-stationary groups under both $\rho$ and $d$; the remaining two require qualification: entropy min's pooled $|\rho|$ (0.40) reflects change concentrated at the gen-0/gen-1 boundary, but for gen-1 vs.\ gen-2+ it is near-stationary ($d{=}0.03$), placing it in the near-stationary group; entropy std shows a substantial level shift ($d{=}0.55$) despite low monotonicity ($|\rho|{=}0.16$), making it the sole intermediate feature.
Entropy min exhibits a discrepancy between location-based (Cohen's $d$\,=\,0.016) and rank-based (Cliff's $\delta$\,=\,0.354) effect sizes, indicating distributional shape change without location shift: recursive generation produces more extreme minimum-entropy tokens while preserving the mean. The near-stationary label refers specifically to location stability; rank-order sensitivity is documented in Appendix~\ref{app:ddr-validation}.
The location/shape decomposition rests on the convergence of $\rho$, Levene, CV shift, and $d$, not the omnibus KS statistic alone.
Per-generator TOST equivalence testing confirms the partition is not a pooling artifact; holdout generator validation confirms stability across two 4/4 splits (Appendix~\ref{app:tost}).
Tail decay shows generator-dependent variation ($d{=}0.15$--$0.22$), but reclassifying it as intermediate preserves the core split and classification performance.

\paragraph{Feature complementarity.}
The full 7-feature set (F1\,=\,0.773) outperforms surface-only (0.688) and reference-only (0.713; McNemar $p \approx 0$; Appendix~\ref{app:ablation-table}).
Permutation importance: hapax ratio (0.35), entropy mean (0.23), TTR (0.18).
PCA confirms the three drifting features share a single latent dimension (92.3\% variance, loadings 0.56--0.59; Appendix~\ref{sec:appendix-feature-correlation}); replacing them with PC1 costs only 1.1\,pp binary F1, and retaining any single drifting feature with the four non-drifting features yields F1\,=\,0.692 (vs.\ 0.701 full).
DDR's contribution is identifying which distributional properties (NLL location vs.\ shape) are depth-sensitive; PC scores achieve equivalent classification but obscure which specific properties drift.
TTR and hapax ratio ($r = 0.97$) show permutation importance differences (0.35 vs.\ 0.18) due to feature masking \cite{strobl_conditional_2008}; all three are retained for marginal LOFO gains (Appendix~\ref{app:lofo}).

\paragraph{Cross-family reference models.}
Alternative references (OLMo-2-1B, Qwen3-0.6B) achieve comparable LOGO F1 (spread 0.013; Table~\ref{tab:cross-ref} in Appendix~\ref{app:cross-ref}), with consistently negative entropy drift.
Pythia generators' highest F1 (0.718--0.724) may partly reflect same-family affinity with the Pythia-410M reference model, but the 0.013 cross-reference spread bounds this effect; depth features are robust to reference model choice, though this does not alone establish DDR as a fundamental property of recursive generation.

\paragraph{Temperature and prompt-type sensitivity.}
The depth signal is modulated by decoding parameters and prompt type (Appendices~\ref{app:sampling-sensitivity},~\ref{app:prompt-type}).
All four tested generators degrade at $t{=}0.9$ ($-9.3$ to $-26.0$\,pp binary F1); low-temperature improvement is model-family-dependent ($+7$--$9$\,pp for Pythia/OLMo at $t{=}0.5$, negligible for Qwen).
Continuation chains show the strongest drift (binary F1\,=\,0.781), with cross-prompt-type transfer confirming shared signal (LOPTO F1\,=\,0.753).
Per-feature convergence trajectories confirm this ordering (Appendix~\ref{app:convergence}); the DDR partition hierarchy is preserved across temperatures despite absolute effect-size compression (Appendix~\ref{app:ddr-temp-stability}).


\subsection{Comparison with Detection Baselines}
\label{sec:results-baselines}

Do existing detection methods already capture depth signal?
To contextualize depth discrimination ability rather than claim competitive advantage, we repurpose four detection scores as ordinal depth predictors using the same XGBoost framework and LOGO splits (Table~\ref{tab:baselines}).

Individual detection scores (N/A) share the reference-model forward pass; per-method timing is not separately profiled.}

The 7-feature ensemble exceeds all individual baselines in 3-class F1 ($\Delta$\,=\,6.7--36.3\,pp).
Multi-detector ensembles achieve marginally higher binary F1 (0.708 vs.\ 0.705) at 2.4$\times$ inference cost; that detection scores achieve comparable depth discrimination suggests depth information is implicitly encoded in distributional divergence measures.
DDR does not outperform detection ensembles on classification; its contribution is decomposing the depth signal into location-sensitive and shape-stable components, enabling analysis of how decoding parameters and instruction tuning modulate each component (\S\ref{sec:discussion}).

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:introduction}

When LLM outputs are fed back as inputs to subsequent generation, the resulting recursive chains form a dynamical system whose distributional properties evolve with each step.
Characterizing the structure of this evolution is fundamental to understanding how base language models transform distributions under iterative conditioning, with relevance to understanding model collapse dynamics \cite{curse_of_recursion, self_consuming_mad}.
Yet binary detection decisions \cite{fast_detectgpt,binoculars,ld_score,detectgpt} obscure this structure: a first-generation continuation retains much of the source distribution's lexical properties, while deeper recursive text exhibits measurably reduced vocabulary diversity and compressed perplexity.

We formulate \emph{generation depth classification}, classifying text by generation depth (gen-0\,/\,gen-1\,/\,gen-2+) rather than a binary label, and term this \emph{depth profiling}.
No existing method provides a feature-level decomposition of depth signal in non-paraphrastic continuation chains.

The key finding is a \emph{differential depth response} (DDR) with a three-way partition: when we measure how eight base-model generators from five families (Pythia, OLMo, Qwen, Llama, Mistral; 0.6B--8B parameters) transform text across recursive depths, three \emph{drifting} features (reference-model mean entropy, type-token ratio, hapax ratio) shift monotonically (Cohen's $d > 0.75$), one \emph{intermediate} feature (entropy std) shows a non-monotonic level shift ($d{=}0.55$), and three \emph{near-stationary} features (entropy max, tail decay, entropy min) exhibit negligible depth effects ($d < 0.10$).
This is consistent with recursive generation shifting the NLL location while distributional shape remains stable under fixed sampling parameters.
While distributional drift under recursive generation is documented in the model collapse literature \cite{curse_of_recursion, self_consuming_mad}, the structured tri-partition and its exploitation for depth classification have not been previously reported.
We restrict to base (pretrained) models: by isolating the generation mechanism from instruction-tuning effects, base models provide a controlled setting in which to study whether recursive distributional drift exhibits systematic structure (\S\ref{sec:discussion}).

A 7-feature ensemble combining all three groups achieves leak-free binary F1\,=\,0.694 under eight-generator leave-one-generator-out (LOGO) evaluation and 0.764 on cross-model chains, using a single 410M-parameter reference model (\S\ref{sec:results-baselines}).

Our contributions are empirical rather than methodological:
\begin{enumerate}[nosep,leftmargin=*]
    \item We formulate generation depth classification, moving beyond binary real-vs-synthetic detection to classify text as gen-0\,/\,gen-1\,/\,gen-2+, and construct an evaluation suite of 37{,}058 texts from eight base-model generators spanning five families (0.6B--8B parameters).
    \item We discover a \emph{differential depth response} (DDR) in base models: data-driven analysis reveals a primary drifting/non-drifting partition ($k{=}2$, silhouette\,=\,0.632); domain-informed criteria further resolve a 3/1/3 characterization (three drifting features, $|\rho| > 0.60$, $d{=}0.76$--$1.17$; one intermediate, $d{=}0.55$; three near-stationary, $d < 0.10$) with a ${\geq}9.5\times$ effect-size gap confirmed under heteroscedasticity-robust metrics (Appendix~\ref{app:ddr-validation}).
    \item We map DDR's boundary conditions: the depth signal is robust within $t \in [0.5, 0.7]$ but attenuates at higher temperatures ($-9.3$ to $-26.0$\,pp at $t{=}0.9$). Instruction tuning compresses the DDR partition structure (silhouette: $0.632 \rightarrow 0.338$) rather than simply reversing feature directions; domain-specific retraining partially recovers within-model classification ($+$7--27\,pp) but cross-generator transfer remains weak (\S\ref{sec:discussion}).
\end{enumerate}

% Abstract — Depth Profiling of Recursive LLM Generation Chains
\begin{abstract}
When large language model (LLM) outputs re-enter the web and seed further generation, how do the statistical properties of the resulting text evolve with each recursive step?
As such text contaminates training corpora, distinguishing generation depth from binary authorship becomes important for data provenance.
We study this question in base (pretrained) models, framing it as \emph{generation depth classification} (gen-0\,/\,gen-1\,/\,gen-2+ rather than binary real-vs-synthetic).
Across eight generators from five families (0.6B--8B parameters), we discover a \emph{differential depth response} (DDR): recursive generation systematically shifts where the negative log-likelihood (NLL) distribution sits under a reference model while leaving its shape largely intact.
This asymmetry yields a stable partition of features into drifting, intermediate, and near-stationary groups.

4	All eight generators are base (pretrained) models.

8	Length-matched analysis yields near-zero correlations ($|\rho| < 0.02$) and binary classification near chance (F1\,$\approx$\,0.5) for Qwen models, leaving interpretation ambiguous.
9	Extending depth profiling to instruct models requires addressing these confounds (length regulation, format constraints, safety-driven distribution shaping) that instruction tuning introduces.
10	
11	Our experiments include generators up to 8.2B parameters (Qwen3-8B).
12	Depth signal persists at this scale (Qwen3-8B 3-class F1\,=\,0.714), but cross-scale transfer incurs a moderate gap vs.\ $\leq$2.8B generators (F1\,=\,0.77--0.81).
13	Frontier models (70B+) and closed-source models remain untested; the consistent scale trend (Mistral-7B binary F1\,=\,0.633, lowest among all generators) suggests depth signal may weaken further at frontier scales, potentially approaching the detection floor.
14	
15	Differential depth response strength is prompt-type dependent: continuation chains show strongest drift (within-type binary F1\,=\,0.781) compared to elaboration (0.730) and rewriting (0.737), with within-prompt-type paraphrastic chains showing weaker signal (binary F1\,=\,0.671 vs.\ 0.749 for within-prompt-type continuation).
16	DDR is most reliably detected in continuation-style generation; near-paraphrastic settings approach the method's detection floor.
17	Cross-prompt-type transfer (LOPTO F1\,=\,0.753) confirms shared signal, yet additional prompt types (e.g., summarization, instruction following) and cross-generator $\times$ cross-prompt interactions remain untested.
18

20	Simulated human editing (\S\ref{sec:discussion}) suggests graceful degradation, but the gap between simulated token replacement and real-world post-processing remains untested.
21	
22	Independent-seed validation covers two of eight generators (Pythia-2.8B and Pythia-1B); extending to all generators, particularly Mistral-7B (lowest LOGO F1), would strengthen seed-independence claims.
23	
24	The reference model is fixed to Pythia-410M throughout, although cross-family reference experiments (\S\ref{sec:results-differential}) confirm the phenomenon is not reference-specific (spread 0.013 across three references).

29

Our primary evaluation uses single-generator chains; cross-model chains (\S\ref{sec:results-classification}) confirm depth signal under generator heterogeneity (3-class F1\,=\,0.809, binary F1\,=\,0.764), though the eight generators represent a controlled laboratory setting rather than the full diversity of real-world contamination.
Simulated human editing (\S\ref{sec:discussion}) suggests graceful degradation, but the gap between simulated token replacement and real-world post-processing remains untested.

Independent-seed validation covers two of eight generators (Pythia-2.8B and Pythia-1B); extending to all generators, particularly Mistral-7B (lowest LOGO F1), would strengthen seed-independence claims.

The reference model is fixed to Pythia-410M throughout, although cross-family reference experiments (\S\ref{sec:results-differential}) confirm the phenomenon is not reference-specific (spread 0.013 across three references).
All seed texts in the main evaluation are English Wikipedia excerpts.
Cross-domain evaluation (Appendix~\ref{app:domain}) at both $t{=}1.0$ and $t{=}0.7$ shows that depth signal persists across News, Academic, and Code domains (binary F1 0.63--0.75 depending on domain and temperature), though a domain $\times$ temperature interaction exists: at $t{=}0.7$, Academic domain binary F1 drops to 0.628, suggesting that reference model calibration is critical for cross-domain deployment.
The reference model dependency (Pythia-410M, English-centric pretraining) limits non-English applicability and adds inference overhead relative to surface-feature-only approaches.
Generalization to other languages remains untested.

Our default analysis uses fixed decoding parameters (temperature 0.7, nucleus $p{=}0.9$). A temperature ablation across four generators from three families (Appendix~\ref{app:sampling-sensitivity}) shows that the method operates reliably within $t \in [0.5, 0.7]$ but degrades at $t{=}0.9$ ($-9.3$ to $-26.0$\,pp across generators). Low-temperature improvement is model-dependent (Pythia/OLMo: $+7$--$9$\,pp; Qwen: $0$--$2$\,pp), indicating that depth profiling assumes standard decoding regimes and that the benefit of conservative temperature varies by model family.
Tokenizer differences across families may contribute to the observed temperature sensitivity pattern; within-family comparisons (two Qwen models showing consistent robustness) support a family-level effect, but controlling for tokenizer requires further study.

Simpler features (character or word n-gram frequencies) were not explored; they may capture complementary surface-level patterns but would not contribute to the location/shape decomposition central to this analysis.

We use 3-class granularity (gen-0\,/\,gen-1\,/\,gen-2+). A 5-class evaluation (Appendix~\ref{app:finer-depth}) yields LOGO F1\,$\approx$\,0.50, with depths 2--4 mutually indistinguishable, validating the 3-class design as the practical resolution limit.
